Snapchat Scam UK: Fake Messages & Impersonation

Scammers are using Snapchat to impersonate the company itself, steal login details, and run money-flipping and romance fraud schemes.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-08-18 · 9 min read

Quick answer: Snapchat itself does not ask for passwords, payment details, or personal ID via message. If you receive such a request, it is a scam. Do not reply or click links. Report the account to Snapchat and block the sender immediately.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What Snapchat scams look like

Snapchat scams fall into several patterns. The most common is a fake verification message claiming your account has been locked or flagged for suspicious activity, asking you to confirm your password, email, or payment details. Another widespread type is romance fraud, where scammers build a relationship with you over weeks or months before asking for money for an emergency, travel, or a business opportunity. A third pattern is money-flipping schemes, where someone claims they can double your money if you send them a small amount first.

Some scammers also pose as Snapchat support staff offering to unlock accounts or restore deleted photos in exchange for payment. All of these lean on Snapchat's disappearing messages, which delete after viewing and can make a conversation harder to evidence. That does not mean nothing survives: Snap says a report made from inside the app can include the reported chat and the messages sent just before it, so report from the conversation itself rather than assuming it has gone. The scammers often target younger users who may be less familiar with how the real Snapchat operates.

How to spot a Snapchat scam message

  • The message asks for your password, email address, phone number, or payment card details. Snapchat's own guidance on password safety says its representatives will never need your password.
  • The sender claims your account is locked, suspended, or flagged and demands immediate action. A genuine lock appears when you try to log in through the app itself, not as a message from another account.
  • You are asked to click a link to verify your identity or log in again. Snapchat does not send login links to you inside Snapchat.
  • The message offers to unlock your account, restore deleted content, or boost your followers for a fee. These are not Snapchat services.
  • A new contact you do not know well is asking for money for an emergency, investment, or travel. This is a classic romance or advance-fee scam.
  • The sender says they are from Snapchat support. Support does not open a conversation with you out of the blue — reach it yourself from Settings inside the app or from Snapchat's help site.
  • The message uses poor grammar, spelling errors, or awkward phrasing. Many scammers operate from outside the UK and their English may be noticeably off.
  • You are asked to move the conversation to another app like WhatsApp, Telegram, or Instagram. Scammers do this to get away from Snapchat's own reporting tools.

How the scam unfolds from first contact

A typical Snapchat scam begins with either a direct message from an unknown account or a message that appears to come from Snapchat itself. If it is a fake verification scam, the message will claim your account needs urgent attention and include a link or instructions to log in or provide details. If you click the link, you land on a fake login page that looks like Snapchat but is actually controlled by the scammer. Anything you enter is captured immediately. In romance scams, the process is slower.

A scammer creates a fake profile, often using stolen photos, and begins chatting with you. Over weeks or months, they build trust and emotional connection. Once they have your confidence, they introduce a problem: they need money for a flight to visit you, medical bills, business investment, or to pay off a debt. They may ask you to send money via bank transfer, gift cards, or cryptocurrency. In money-flipping schemes, the scammer shows you screenshots of supposed earnings and promises to multiply your investment. Once you send money, they disappear.

Disappearing messages make all of this harder to evidence after the fact, which is part of why scammers favour the app — but they do not wipe the slate. Snap says an in-app report can carry the reported chat and the messages immediately before it, so report from inside the conversation, and screenshot what you can while you can.

How to check if a message is really from Snapchat

Do not try to work out whether an account contacting you is really Snapchat — go to support yourself instead, and the question does not arise. Open Snapchat, tap your profile icon, open the settings gear and choose Support, which takes you into Snapchat's own help centre. Snapchat's published guidance on keeping your password safe is explicit that its representatives will never need your password, so a message asking you to confirm one is a scam however official it looks — and the same goes for any message asking you to verify your account or hand over payment details.

If you receive a suspicious message claiming to be from Snapchat, do not click any links or reply. Instead, report the account directly within Snapchat by opening the message, tapping the three dots, and selecting Report. If you are unsure whether your account has a real problem, log out of Snapchat completely and log back in using the official app. A genuine lock shows up at that point, not in a message from another user, and Snapchat's own account-lock guidance sets out the recovery routes from there.

What to do if you have already sent money or shared details

If you have sent money via bank transfer, contact your bank immediately and explain that you have been the victim of fraud. Ask them to attempt to recall the payment. An eligible payment sent by Faster Payments or CHAPS from a UK account on or after 7 October 2024 may be covered by the mandatory reimbursement rules for authorised push payment fraud: you have 13 months to claim, reimbursement is capped at £85,000, exclusions apply, and your firm may deduct an excess of up to £100 — though it cannot apply that excess to a consumer it assesses as vulnerable.

Ask your bank to assess the claim and tell you what evidence it needs. If you sent money via gift cards or cryptocurrency, the situation is more difficult because these transactions are usually irreversible, but report it to the platform where you bought the cards or crypto, as they may be able to freeze the account. If you have shared your password, email address, or phone number, change your Snapchat password immediately using a device the scammer does not have access to. Enable two-factor authentication on your Snapchat account and on the email address linked to it.

Check your account activity for any unauthorised logins or changes. If you have shared your bank details or card number, contact your bank and ask them to monitor your account for fraudulent transactions. If you are worried your identity will be misused, the UK mechanism is Cifas Protective Registration, which costs £30, runs for two years, and asks lenders to carry out extra checks before granting credit in your name — apply at cifas.org.uk/pr.

You can also request your statutory credit report free of charge from the agencies MoneyHelper lists — Experian, Equifax and TransUnion, the three main ones, plus Crediva — and check it for accounts you did not open.

How to report a Snapchat scam in the UK

Report the scam to Snapchat first by opening the message, tapping the three dots, and selecting Report. Snap says reports are reviewed against its Community Guidelines and can lead to enforcement action on the account, which may mean a warning, a restriction, or removal. Then report the scam to the appropriate UK authority depending on where you live. In England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, report it to Report Fraud by calling 0300 123 2040 or visiting https://www.reportfraud.police.uk. In Scotland, report it to Police Scotland on 101 or via https://www.scotland.police.uk/contact-us/non-emergencies/.

If the scam involved a fake login page or any other suspicious website, send the address to the National Cyber Security Centre using its report a suspicious website form at https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/section/about-this-website/report-scam-website. Its Suspicious Email Reporting Service mailbox is a separate route for suspicious emails and is not the place for a website. If you received a scam SMS or text message, forward it to 7726, the shortcode run by the mobile networks.

For consumer advice and support, contact Citizens Advice consumer helpline on 0808 223 1133 if you are in England or Wales, Advice Direct Scotland on 0808 800 9060 if you are in Scotland, or Consumerline on 0300 123 6262 if you are in Northern Ireland. Keep a record of the scammer's username, the date and time of the messages, and any screenshots you took before the messages disappeared.

Frequently asked questions

Is a message asking me to verify my Snapchat account real?

No. Snapchat does not ask you to verify your account via direct message. If your account has a genuine issue, you will see a notification when you log in through the official app, or you can check your account settings. Any message asking you to click a link or provide your password is a scam. Report the account and block the sender.

Someone on Snapchat is asking me to send money. Are they real?

Almost certainly not. Scammers use Snapchat to build fake relationships and then ask for money for emergencies, travel, or investments. If you have only known someone for a short time and they are asking for money, it is a scam. Do not send anything. Block them and report the account to Snapchat.

I clicked a link in a Snapchat message and entered my password. What should I do?

Change your Snapchat password immediately from a different device. Enable two-factor authentication on your Snapchat account and on the email address linked to it. Monitor your account for any unauthorised activity. If the link also asked for your email or phone number, change the password on those accounts too and check for any suspicious activity.

Can Snapchat recover my account if a scammer has taken it over?

Yes, but you need to act quickly. Go to Snapchat's support page through the app or website and report that your account has been hacked. Provide as much information as you can about your account, such as your username, email, and phone number. Snapchat will help you regain access. Change your password as soon as you can.

What should I do if I sent money to a scammer on Snapchat?

Contact your bank immediately and report the fraud. Ask them to attempt to recall the payment and to assess a reimbursement claim: an eligible Faster Payments or CHAPS transfer sent on or after 7 October 2024 falls under the mandatory APP reimbursement rules, with a 13-month claim window, an £85,000 cap, and a possible excess of up to £100 that cannot be charged to a consumer the firm assesses as vulnerable. Report the scam to Report Fraud (0300 123 2040 in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland) or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. Report the Snapchat account to Snapchat itself. If you sent money via gift cards or cryptocurrency, report it to the platform where you bought them.
